title: Seeing Beyond the Next Step: World-Model-Guided Human-Like Navigation in Multi-Agent Scenes
claim: A two-stage training pipeline distills world-model foresight into a policy by scoring candidate actions with predicted consequences.
layout: 2 regions, left-to-right stages with arrows; right panel details world models
description: The figure has two parts, separated by a dashed pink vertical line. The left part starts with a blue Observation bar made of four inputs: an RGB frame, an ego-relative goal icon, ego-relative velocities, and nearby pedestrians and dynamic objects. Blue arrows run down into two orange-shaded stage boxes. Stage 1 (Traditional VLA Training) has a VLM with a LoRA flame icon feeding an Anchor box. Stage 2 (Future-Consequence Preference Learning) has a VLM with LoRA feeding a Candidate Group box. Candidate Group connects to a red World Model box, then a green Predicted Future Outcomes box, then a blue Preference-Guided GRPO box that loops back to the candidates. The right part expands the pieces. A red box holds State Transition and Semantic Transition world models. A green box shows predicted velocity and position and a semantic image. A blue box lists the reward terms: goal progress, smoothness, current and future risk, and semantic validity. Color coding links the two parts, with red, green and blue repeated.
caption: Overview of the proposed training pipeline. In Stage 1, we adapt a pretrained VLM into a VLA policy through supervised learning, grounding agent-centric visual observations and structured navigation context to executable motion-skill actions. In Stage 2, we further refine the policy with dual world models, which teaches the agent action--outcome knowledge by comparing plausible candidate actions according to their predicted social, semantic, and goal-directed consequences.
abstract: Selecting a next motion in a populated scene is not just a matter of avoiding what is currently in the way: an action can be locally feasible yet drift onto the road instead of the crosswalk, cut into a stream of crossing pedestrians, or bottleneck a narrow passage. These failure modes are invisible from the current state alone, and acting on them requires reasoning about what each candidate action will cause. World models offer exactly this, namely action-conditioned predictions of the future, but rolling them out at every decision step is a cost deployable navigation systems cannot pay, and the field has largely traded foresight for speed. We argue this is a false dichotomy. The natural place for a world model in human-aware navigation is at training time, as a preference oracle that distills foresight into a fast policy, rather than at inference time, as an online planner. We pair a discrete visual action prior with two task-aligned world models, one for nearby social dynamics and one for future scene semantics, that score candidate actions by their predicted consequences and refine the policy through group-relative preference distillation. At deployment, both world models are removed and the policy acts in a single forward pass. Across five held-out evaluation scenarios, this yields navigation that is simultaneously safer, more socially and group-coherent, and more goal-directed than strong reactive and learned baselines, with naive observers rating the resulting motion as more human-like. Taken together, our findings point to a different approach for bringing world-model foresight into deployable agents: not accelerating rollouts, but amortizing them into the policy so that the cost of looking ahead is confined to training.
